g: Popular history of philosophy; biographical survey
sum: Will Durant walks through the Western philosophical tradition one great figure at a time: Plato, Aristotle, Bacon, Spinoza, Voltaire, Kant, Schopenhauer, Spencer, Nietzsche and a closing chapter on American thinkers. Each chapter pairs a life story with a lucid account of the ideas, written to make readers want the originals.
bg: Developed from lectures and pamphlets for working adults, the book was published in 1926 and became one of the first runaway bestsellers about philosophy, funding Durant’s later multi-volume Story of Civilization. Durant later won a Pulitzer Prize with his wife Ariel for a volume of The Story of Civilization.
br: Use it as a companion rather than a substitute: read Durant’s chapter on a thinker just before or after you tackle that thinker’s own book elsewhere in your plan.
la: Durant is openly enthusiastic and opinionated; he favours narrative, telling quotation and biography, and is not shy about which philosophers he loves (Spinoza) or distrusts. His sentences are quotable and often witty.
cx: The selection reflects a 1920s Western canon: medieval, women and non-Western philosophers are absent, and some judgments have been revised by later scholarship. Read it as a period piece as well as a guide.
th: Ideas grow from lives
Durant shows how temperament and circumstance shape a philosophy.
Philosophy for everyone
He insists big questions belong to general readers, not only specialists.
The making of a canon
Who is included tells us what an era thought philosophy was.
fit: A friendly map for the Plato, Spinoza, Kant and Nietzsche titles already in your plan, and pleasant to read in short sittings.
mis: Dated in places, narrowly Western, and inclined to simplify; specialists find it romantic.
cw: Period-typical remarks on gender and race in a few passages.
rq: Which thinker does Durant make most alive, and how?
Where do you sense him taking sides?
Who would you add to the book today?
dq: What do we gain and lose when philosophy is told as biography?
Has reading Durant made a primary text easier or harder to approach?
rel: Durant’s favourite, Spinoza, in his own words.

g: Philosophy of science; Very Short Introduction
sum: Samir Okasha explains what makes science distinctive and why its methods are philosophically puzzling. Short chapters cover inductive reasoning, explanation, whether theories describe an unseen reality, Kuhn’s scientific revolutions, and conceptual debates in physics, biology and psychology. A closing chapter considers science and its critics.
bg: Part of Oxford University Press’s Very Short Introductions, first published in 2002 and updated in a second edition in 2016. Okasha is a philosopher of biology at the University of Bristol. It is often recommended as a first introduction to the subject for students and general readers alike.
br: Small but dense: read a chapter at a time and keep a note of key terms such as induction, falsifiability, underdetermination and paradigm. Each chapter ends with a clear summary, and there is a short guide to further reading.
la: Okasha presents each debate even-handedly, setting out positions and objections with everyday and historical examples rather than formal logic. Debates are framed as live questions rather than settled answers, and the tone is patient and encouraging throughout.
cx: The book introduces the arguments of Hume, Popper and Kuhn and later debates about realism, and touches on public controversies such as creationism. Examples range from Copernicus and Newton to modern genetics.
th: The problem of induction
Our confidence that the future will resemble the past is hard to justify.
Realism and anti-realism
Do electrons and genes exist as theories describe them?
How science changes
Revolutions may replace one way of seeing with another.
fit: A thinking toolkit for the many science and psychology titles on your plan, especially when they disagree.
mis: Very compressed; readers who want history or narrative may find it dry. It is an overview, not a story.
rq: Why can’t Popper’s falsification fully solve induction?
What does Kuhn mean by normal science?
Which scientific entities do you take to be real, and why?
dq: Is science objective if scientists are shaped by paradigms?
How should non-experts decide which scientists to trust?
rel: Sagan’s practical defence of scientific thinking.

sum: Nine stories pose quiet, rigorous thought experiments: a mechanical being studying its own brain, a merchant passing through a gate in time, a woman raising digital creatures over many years, and a device that proves free will is an illusion. Each turns an idea into a question about how to live.
bg: Ted Chiang’s second collection, published in 2019, gathers stories from 2005 onward, including the award-winning The Merchant and the Alchemist’s Gate, the title story Exhalation and the novella The Lifecycle of Software Objects. Several stories first appeared in anthologies and magazines.
br: Read one story per sitting and leave a pause; several are best digested before moving on. Each stands alone. The title story is short; the novella is the longest piece, so give it a quiet evening of its own.
la: Chiang writes clean, unshowy prose and builds each story from a single premise followed to its moral consequences, often in forms such as a confession, a lab notebook or a fable.
cx: Chiang publishes rarely and works as a technical writer; his stories are frequently discussed in debates about artificial intelligence, determinism and ethics. His story Story of Your Life became the film Arrival.
th: Free will and fate
Knowing the future need not cancel the meaning of our choices.
Entropy and mortality
Every system, including us, runs down, and that can be faced with grace.
Care for created minds
Raising a mind is a moral relationship rather than a product cycle.
fit: Joins your philosophy and science shelves in fiction form, and pairs well with Exhalation-style questions in Determined and Behave.
mis: Readers wanting action, vivid characters or sustained plot may find the stories cerebral and calm.
cw: Grief, loss of a child (in one story), existential dread.
rq: Which story changed how you think about choice?
How does the narrator of Exhalation make discovery feel?
What do the digients deserve from their keepers?
dq: Is Chiang an optimist about technology?
Which premise would you most like to see as a novel?

sum: Carl Sagan argues that science is the best tool we have for not fooling ourselves. He examines alien abductions, faith healing, witch hunts and pseudoscience, offers a baloney detection kit for testing claims, and makes a moving case that scientific thinking and democracy depend on each other.
bg: Published in 1995, shortly before Sagan’s death in 1996, and written with his collaborator Ann Druyan, it is often called his most personal and urgent book. Its subtitle is Science as a Candle in the Dark, and it remains in print and widely recommended.
br: The chapters are independent; the baloney detection kit chapter is worth rereading. Keep a recent claim from the news in mind as you go. Chapters are self-contained. The final chapters on democracy are the most personal.
la: Sagan combines anecdote, history and plain argument, with warmth rather than contempt for people who believe strange things. Humour and personal memory, including stories of his parents, soften the argument and make it warm rather than lecturing.
cx: Written amid concern over declining science literacy in the United States; many of its warnings about misinformation are now read as prescient. Its warnings now feel prescient.
th: Sceptical tools
Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence, and anyone can learn to ask for it.
Wonder and rigour
Science is a source of awe, not only of doubt and debunking.
Science and freedom
Free inquiry and public reason sustain democracy, and each protects the other.
fit: A foundation for your science shelf and a practical companion to the psychology books on bias.
mis: Some examples feel of their time, and the tone can be preachy for already-convinced readers.
rq: Which baloney detection tool will you actually use?
Why does Sagan treat believers with sympathy?
Where do you see his warnings today?
dq: Is scepticism enough to defeat misinformation?
What responsibility do scientists have to the public?
rel: Self-justification and why we resist evidence.

g: Popular science; astronomy and the history of science
sum: Carl Sagan surveys the universe from the Big Bang to the evolution of life and intelligence on Earth, telling the stories of the people who worked it out, from Eratosthenes and Kepler to the Voyager missions. Science becomes a human adventure and a reason to care for our small world.
bg: Published in 1980 to accompany the television series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, it became one of the best-selling science books ever written in English. Sagan, an astronomer at Cornell, worked on NASA missions including Viking and Voyager, so many of the discoveries he describes were ones he helped make.
br: Read a chapter at a time; pairing chapters with the original series is a pleasure if you can find it. Illustrated editions add a great deal. Start with chapter one, The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean.
la: Sagan moves between cosmic scale and intimate human moments, mixing explanation with lyrical reflection. His famous phrases, such as we are made of star-stuff, come from this book and series, and the writing has a deliberate cadence meant to be spoken.
cx: Written during the Cold War and early planetary exploration; its warnings about nuclear war and environmental damage frame the closing chapters. Its sense of urgency feels current.
th: Cosmic perspective
Seeing our place in the universe changes our priorities and our sense of kinship.
The history of discovery
Knowledge is a hard-won human story full of persecution and courage.
Stewardship
Intelligence brings responsibility for the only planet we know has life.
fit: A wonder-filled classic that balances the denser science titles on your plan. It is also simply beautiful to read.
mis: Some scientific details are dated, and the lyrical tone is not to every taste.
rq: Which historical figure did Sagan bring to life for you?
What has science learned since 1980?
How does he make vast numbers feel real?
dq: Is the cosmic perspective comforting or unsettling?
What should popular science aim to do?
rel: Sagan’s later reflection on our place in space.

g: Popular science; evolution and the argument from design
sum: Why do living things look designed? Dawkins shows how cumulative natural selection, small advantageous changes preserved over immense time, can build eyes, wings and bat echolocation without a designer. He explains why evolution is the opposite of random chance and weighs rival theories of how it works.
bg: Published in 1986, the title answers William Paley’s 1802 argument that a watch implies a watchmaker and a living organism implies God. It won the Royal Society of Literature’s Heinemann Award. It remains one of his most widely read books.
br: Reads well after The Selfish Gene but stands alone. The chapter on bats and the computer biomorph experiments are highlights. Illustrations of the biomorphs help. No technical background is needed.
la: Dawkins argues step by step with analogies, numbers and simulations, and does not hide his combative opinions. The famous calculation about how quickly selection could produce a line of Shakespeare makes the case vivid and memorable for non-specialists.
cx: Written during disputes over creationism in American schools and debates among biologists about punctuated equilibrium; it remains a classic popular defence of Darwinian gradualism. Read it alongside critics for balance.
th: Cumulative selection
Tiny steps, kept and compounded over time, add up to astonishing complexity.
The appearance of design
Natural processes can convincingly mimic purpose and design.
Explanation and wonder
Understanding a mechanism can deepen awe rather than destroy it.
fit: The clearest single explanation of how evolution builds complexity, useful background for Behave and The Gene.
mis: The polemical edge toward religious belief may irritate, and some debates have moved on.
rq: Why is evolution not random chance?
What does the biomorph program demonstrate?
What does Paley get right about living things?
dq: Is design thinking a natural human bias?
Does this argument settle anything about religion?

g: Science journalism; extinction and environmental change
sum: Elizabeth Kolbert argues that we are living through the sixth mass extinction in Earth’s history, and the first caused by a single species. Each chapter follows one creature, from the Panamanian golden frog to the Sumatran rhino, and the scientists tracking its fate, interleaved with the history of how extinction itself came to be understood.
bg: Kolbert, a staff writer at The New Yorker, won the 2015 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for the book. She had earlier written Field Notes from a Catastrophe, about climate change, and the book grew out of her magazine reporting.
br: Chapters work as linked essays; read one at a time. The opening chapter on frogs sets the method. Endnotes point to the scientific sources, and the chapters build a cumulative case across eras and continents.
la: Kolbert’s style is calm, precise and wry; she lets carefully chosen facts carry the emotional force rather than heightening them. Each chapter pairs a historical idea with a present-day field trip, which gives the book unusual shape and momentum.
cx: The book connects Cuvier, Lyell and Darwin’s debates about extinction with modern ocean acidification, climate change, invasive species and habitat fragmentation. It explains the term Anthropocene, the proposed age of human influence, for general readers.
th: Humans as geological force
Our species now shapes the planet’s history like an asteroid or ice age.
How extinction was discovered
The very idea that species could vanish was once deeply controversial.
Quiet loss
Most extinctions happen quietly, without anyone noticing at all.
fit: Gives scientific depth to environmental questions and pairs with Entangled Life and An Immense World.
mis: Sobering and largely diagnostic; readers wanting solutions or hope will find little. Its restraint can feel cold to some.
cw: Ecological grief; animal death and suffering.
rq: Which species’ story affected you most?
How did scientists come to accept extinction?
Which human activity worries you most after reading?
dq: What do we owe species we will never see?
Is it still possible to be hopeful about the planet?
rel: A more celebratory look at living networks.

sum: Merlin Sheldrake explores fungi, a kingdom that sustains most plant life through underground networks, digests rock and pollutants, makes bread and alcohol possible, and alters minds. Along the way he asks what fungi teach us about intelligence, cooperation and the boundaries of the individual. It is a celebration of interdependence.
bg: Published in 2020, Entangled Life won the Royal Society Science Book Prize in 2021. Sheldrake is a biologist whose doctoral research studied mycorrhizal networks in Panama. His brother Cosmo is a musician, and his father Rupert Sheldrake is a biologist known for controversial theories, though Merlin’s book stays within mainstream science.
br: Expect digressions and personal experiments: Sheldrake ferments, forages and grows mushrooms on his own book. Enjoy the meandering. Notes and references are extensive, and an illustrated edition is available.
la: Sheldrake mixes laboratory science, history, anecdote and philosophy in a voice full of curiosity, often pausing to ask what metaphors we use for living things and why. His enthusiasm is contagious.
cx: The book discusses the much-debated wood wide web idea and psychedelic research, areas where popular enthusiasm sometimes outruns evidence. Fungi’s role in climate and soil health gives it urgency.
th: Entanglement
Organisms live through relationships, not alone, and fungi make that visible.
Rethinking the individual
Lichens and underground networks blur where one life ends and another begins.
Attention to the overlooked
The hidden world under our feet is extraordinary when we attend to it.
fit: A joyful, wonder-filled science read that balances the bleaker environmental titles. It pairs naturally with An Immense World on your list.
mis: Some claims are speculative, and the discursive style can feel unfocused. Its digressions will suit some readers more than others.
rq: Which fungal fact most surprised you?
How do lichens challenge the idea of a single organism?
Where does Sheldrake flag uncertainty?
dq: How would seeing yourself as entangled change your choices?
When do metaphors help or hurt science?
rel: Another book about perceiving non-human worlds.
